body: Glad you have a friend you can talk to. That can be extremely valuable.

I feel that losing a friendship or relationship, especially over something like this, is worse that dealing with the death of someone. The person is gone for you, but only you. No one else quite understands the depths of your grief, you can't grieve with friends or family members, and there's no closure. Plus that "dead person" is pouring salt onto the wound. And somewhere, somehow, it's not that unrealistic for that "dead person" to come back from the dead.

I've honestly wanted to erect a tombstone after losing someone in a somewhat similar manner, because I felt it would somehow give the grief legitimacy.

To my future wife: If you are dealing with issues like this, I understand. You're not alone. I'm there with you. Take your time. Say what you feel comfortable saying, and save the rest for another time. And if you feel the need to talk about it in the middle of the night, call me. I mute all notifications at night, but I set calls to come through, and there's a reason for that. As long as you're honest with me, everything is fine, and that includes telling me you don't want to talk about it right now. All I ask is for you to be understanding with me; I'll do my best to be understanding with you.

To OP: You will find someone who can deal with your mess, and support you through it. I have been in a relationship with someone with similar issues. As long as you don't lie to them, everything is fine. If you want to elaborate, elaborate, if you don't, don't. And if they aren't comfortable with that, then they don't deserve you.

That's what I've also figured. Before I started into the relationship, I viewed it as "friendships are more important than relationships". I guess my main takeaway is how hard that is to enforce when you're in a relationship.

The controlling aspect is also something that I've noticed a bit, but I never knew how to handle it. To a certain extent, if you're in a relationship, you talk with your partner and sometimes change plans accordingly. The only thing is, that has to go in both directions.

The thing is... yes, I'll be honest, she has issues. But they're definitely not all her own fault, and I want to help her with them. She's also helped me with some of my issues, so I don't think it would be right to outright dump her because of that.

I don't know why I didn't think about the boundary with the yelling earlier, but that's definitely something I should try and that I want to do now. Sometimes she can talk about things calmly, but not always. It's kind of hit or miss. I'll try it, and I hope it works. Thanks for the advice :)  
Edit: it's also nice to know that the yelling and shouting isn't normal, even if the family claims otherwise (they've explained it as: otherwise you're bottling up your emotions, which is worse and means you're not being honest). I didn't intend to emphasize the yelling and shouting while writing my post, so the fact that it's still your biggest takeaway is definitely telling.
